subject: principles-of-management
name: Principles of Management
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance).

units.title: Organisations and Introduction to Management
topics: Managerial hierarchy and types of managers

sections.title: Managerial hierarchy and types of managers

summary: An organisation is a structured group pursuing common goals; effective goals are SMART, accepted and consistent; goals can be displaced or succeeded.
Management is the process of planning, organising, leading and controlling to achieve goals efficiently and effectively; it is universal, goal-directed and both an art and a science.
Fayol's fourteen principles guide structure and behaviour as flexible rules.
There are three levels of managers needing different mixes of technical, human and conceptual skills; Mintzberg describes ten roles.
Globalisation, technology, diversity, ethics and change are the main challenges.

units.title: Evolution of Management Thought and the Environment
topics: Human relations and behavioural science theories
System, decision, management science and contingency theories

sections.title: Human relations and behavioural science theories
System, decision, management science and contingency theories

summary: Classical thinkers (Taylor, Fayol, Weber) sought efficiency through method, principles and rules; the Hawthorne studies and behavioural scientists discovered people's social and psychological needs.
Systems, decision, management-science and contingency theories add holistic, rational, quantitative and situational views — no single best way.
Diversity, outsourcing, knowledge management and learning organisations are current concepts.
Organisations operate in internal, task and general environments; scanning economic, socio-cultural, political and technological factors guides decisions, including in Nepal's changing context.
Social responsibility and business ethics are now part of managerial duty.

units.title: Planning and Decision Making
summary: Planning gives direction and a basis for control; strategic, tactical and operational plans fit into a hierarchy from mission to rules; the planning process runs from premises to evaluated, controlled implementation.
MBO makes planning participative; strategic planning uses environmental scanning and SWOT.
Break-even, decision trees, PERT/CPM and EOQ are practical quantitative tools.
Decisions are programmed or non-programmed and made under certainty, risk or uncertainty, each with its own criteria; real managers satisfice.
Problem solving finds root causes with fishbone, 5 Whys and Pareto analysis.

units.title: Organising
topics: Span of management and organisation shape
Organic and mechanistic organisations (Burns and Stalker)

sections.title: Span of management and organisation shape
Organic and mechanistic organisations (Burns and Stalker)

summary: Organising divides work, groups it into departments, assigns authority and responsibility and coordinates people through a structure.
Classical, behavioural and contingency views give different designs; the choice depends on the situation.
Span of management shapes tall or flat structures; Graicunas shows why spans are limited.
Line authority commands, staff authority advises; delegation passes authority but not accountability; decentralisation spreads authority by policy and devolution transfers it fully.
Mechanistic structures suit stable environments, organic ones turbulent; matrix, team and network structures answer modern needs.

units.title: Leading: Leadership, Motivation and Communication
summary: Leadership influences people to pursue goals; trait, behavioural and situational approaches explain it, and the best style adapts to followers and tasks.
Groups pass through predictable stages and are shaped by norms and cohesion; conflict can be constructive when managed with the right mode.
Motivation theories — Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor, Vroom, equity — guide rewards, job enrichment, participation and self-managed teams.
Communication is a two-way process of encoding, transmitting, decoding and feedback; barriers are semantic, physical, psychological and organisational; active listening and feedback improve it.

units.title: Controlling, Quality and the Global Context
topics: Characteristics of an effective control system
Management trends and scenario in Nepal

sections.title: Characteristics of an effective control system
Management trends and scenario in Nepal

summary: Control compares performance with standards and corrects deviations; feedforward, concurrent and feedback controls act before, during and after the work; effective control is timely, economical, flexible and accepted.
Tools include budgets and variance, ratios, audits, Gantt/PERT, control charts and inventory control.
Quality is meeting customer needs; TQM involves everyone in continuous improvement using the seven basic tools, Deming's PDCA and 14 points, Kaizen, Six Sigma and 5S.
Globalisation brings opportunities and challenges that demand cultural intelligence.

Nepal's management scene is shifting from family-run, relationship-based practice to more professional, digital and quality-conscious management, against infrastructure, political and skill-shortage challenges.

sections.title: Managing ethics and diversity, and social responsibility (revision map)
The role of IT in management
Job analysis, job design, job description and job specification
Authority distribution and forms of organisational design
Approaches to leadership: generic, situational and emerging
Managing teams in a time of crisis
Leadership challenges in an IT-based organisation

summary: A form of business is chosen by liability, capital, control and continuity; companies give limited liability and perpetual succession, sole traders and general partners carry unlimited liability.
The integrated framework shows management as skills, roles and functions inside an environment, steered by ethics and supported by IT.

IT supports planning, decision making, organising, leading and controlling; it helps structured decisions most and unstructured decisions least, and a cost-benefit view (payback) tests an IT purchase.
Job analysis produces the description and the specification; job design ranges from simplification to enrichment and the job characteristics model.
Organisational design may be functional, divisional, matrix, team, network or virtual, each with a trade-off.
Leadership theories moved from traits to behaviour, to situation, to transformation and service; no single style is best, and a crisis calls for calm, directive and honest leadership.
IT organisations ask for leaders who combine vision, trust in experts, care for people and a firm ethical line.
